item.title: Ada/Calvo win Adelup; Limtiaco new delegate; Tydingco wins AG race; Republican majority in Legislature
item.description: Republicans Tony Ada and E.J. Calvo were elected as the new governor and lieutenant governor of Guam on Tuesday. Democrat Alicia Limtiaco defeated incumbent Republican Del. James Moylan in the race for Congress.
item.content:encoded:
Republicans Tony Ada and E.J. Calvo were elected as the new governor and lieutenant governor of Guam on Tuesday.

Democrat Alicia Limtiaco defeated incumbent Republican Del. James Moylan in the race for Congress.

Phillip Tydingco beat incumbent Doug Moylan in the race for attorney general.

In the legislative race, Republicans took the majority of seats, with eight to the seven held by Democrats.

Legislative winners were: Chris Barnett (i) (DEM) Amanda Shelton (DEM) Sabrina Salas Matanane (i) (REP) Jesse Lujan (i) (REP) Chris Duenas (i) (REP) Telena Nelson (DEM) Telo Taitague (i) (REP) Hoa Van Nguyen (REP) William Parkinson (i) (DEM) Donna Quinata (DEM) Clynt Ridgell (DEM) Vince Borja (i) (REP) Shelly Calvo (i) (REP) Kallen Perez (DEM) Eulogio Shawn Gumataotao (i) (REP)

item.title: Guam voters point to cost of living, education and public safety as key election concerns
item.description: Guam voters headed to the polls Tuesday with concerns about the island's cost of living, education, public safety, and the future decisions in this year's general election. In interviews with KPRG News at polling locations across the island, residents shared what motivated them to vote and what they hope the island's next elected leaders will address.
item.content:encoded:
Guam voters headed to the polls Tuesday with concerns about the island's cost of living, education, public safety, and the future decisions in this year's general election.

In interviews with KPRG News at polling locations across the island, residents shared what motivated them to vote and what they hope the island's next elected leaders will address.

For some, rising living expenses remain a major concern. Voters pointed to increasing housing costs, rent and utility bills, along with the need for more employment opportunities and livable wages.

Yona resident Evan San Nicolas said balancing employment and household expenses remains a challenge, regardless of whether someone works in the public, private, or nonprofit sector.

“Some important issues to me are the cost of living,” San Nicolas said. “Ultimately, I am a homeowner, so also tying in employment. Seeing, are we able to find a good job? In every sector of employment, it is such a task to be qualified for it, and the timing of everything too, also blends in towards when our bills are due, that kind of thing.”

Education was another recurring concern, particularly among parents who said the island's children depend on stronger support for schools and teachers.

Cherish Keaunui said her children were her primary motivation for voting. She also raised concerns about the lack of support for teachers and the rising costs of basic living expenses.

“Education is a really big thing. With the lack in support that I’ve seen for teachers, that’s what really pushed me,” Keaunui said. “And then also today with like a lot of the rising costs and living, you know, rent, utilities and stuff, it’s been a big burden. And I know its a big thing on everybody. But today, I really needed to vote because my kids rely on it.”

Public safety and drug abuse were also among the issues voters want the next administration to address.

Mark Alviz said he wants to see greater attention given to the island's safety, including efforts to address Guam's drug problem. “I mean, just how it’s gotten just so bad over the last how many years, just there needs to be change there,” Alviz said. He also expressed concern about Guam's strategic position as a military location and the importance of having leaders who prioritize the island's security. “So I just want to make sure when voting, having the right people that put that as a priority is one quality that I’m looking for,” Alviz said.

Other residents raised concerns about government services and accountability.

Vince Flores of Agana Heights pointed to challenges facing the education system and hospital, as well as government spending, procurement, and transparency. He said the government needs to find ways to improve services and create more opportunities for residents to own businesses and build their livelihoods on Guam.

“The important issues are education, the education process, and the system right now is always hurting,” Flores said. “It’s like, how is that happening? And other services within the agencies, and we just have too much overhead. They got to think outside the box and provide some assistance somehow, someway.”

For some voters, the election also carried concerns about the future of the island's indigenous population.

Dededo resident and veteran Joe Leon Guerrero said he hopes more CHamoru people will remain on Guam or return home to support their communities. He expressed concern about residents leaving the island and the need to ensure the local population continues to thrive.

“The reason why I’m voting is because our people are dying out and leaving the island,” Leon Guerrero said. “Outsiders are coming in, and one day they’re going to take over if people keep neglecting from voting. So please vote.”

While voters identified different priorities, their responses reflected a shared expectation that the island's next leaders address the challenges affecting residents' everyday lives.

As Guam begins its next election cycle, voters say casting their ballots is one way to make their voices heard on the issues that matter to them.

item.title: For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life
item.description: KHERSON, Ukraine — In this city where Russian drones usually fill the skies, Olena Soboleva could not easily walk down the street to meet her best friend, Anna Herasimenko. Then came last week's truce, negotiated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, in a corner of southern Ukraine that included Kherson.
item.content:encoded:
KHERSON, Ukraine — In this city where Russian drones usually fill the skies, Olena Soboleva could not easily walk down the street to meet her best friend, Anna Herasimenko.

Then came last week's truce, negotiated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, in a corner of southern Ukraine that included Kherson.

This weekend, the two friends, both 21, took the opportunity to venture outside to autumnal skies clear of drones and guided bombs.

"No drones, no explosions," Soboleva says. "No one wants to kill you."

They passed families strolling with their kids, shoppers stocking up on supplies and couples holding hands. They lined up at a cafe filled with paintings of cats.

"The city seems alive," says Herasimenko, "just like it used to be."

Over the weekend, she had also ventured to a salon.

"I did my nails," she says, showing off fresh burgundy polish. "The streets are full of people, just as they were in the past."

The truce ended Sunday night. Russia and Ukraine agreed to it in order to help Oleshky, a town across the Dnipro River from Kherson. Russian troops occupied Oleshky in 2022 and mined the land around it. Food and medicine rarely got through. NPR spoke to the families of residents there, who said their loved ones survived on pickles and boiled weeds.

Over the weekend, hundreds of Oleshky residents were evacuated, eventually escorted into northern Ukraine on buses. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's ombudsman — the country's independent watchdog for human rights — thanked Melania Trump for ensuring that the ceasefire, which lasted from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1, happened.

"I believe they can be upheld and honored," Lubinets said about truces between Ukraine and Russia.

Even a short pause in hostilities was a respite for Kherson. Russian troops occupied the city for several months in 2022, until local partisans spied for Ukrainian soldiers, who then forced the Russians out of the city.

Since 2024, Russian troops based across the river have hunted Kherson residents with FPV (first-person-view) drones strapped with explosives. The highway into Kherson is shrouded in tunnels of heavy mesh nets to protect locals from these drones. These anti-drone nets also cover Kherson's streets and many of its buildings.

This weekend, cars pulled up next to the Greek-style monument marking the city's gateway.

Svitlana Vorobiova, a retired police officer, drove here from a safer city where she now lives. She took photos with her children at the monument.

"I have a place in Kherson, and my parents are also here," she says, and her voice breaks. Tears fill her eyes.

"I brought my son with me," Vorobiova says. "He hasn't been here in four years. He said, 'I cannot believe I'm in my hometown!'"

Inside the city, Volodymyr Mykolaienko, a former mayor of Kherson, strolls past the crushed remains of a once-grand administrative building. Locals stop him and shake his hand. He says he's happy to see so many people outside.

"I walk around the city a lot these days," he says. "I cannot sit still at home."

Mykolaienko, 66, spent years as a prisoner of war in Russia, confined to tiny rooms, starved and tortured. Russian troops arrested him in Kherson in early 2022, when the city was under Russian occupation. Mykolaienko was freed last year in a prisoner exchange and returned to Kherson, where his family still lives.

This truce allowed him to visit his father's grave. The cemetery is in a part of the city that's usually filled with drones.

"I could not hold myself back," he says. "I was able to do exactly what I have long wanted to do — to talk to my father, pray, thank him for my life and to tell him what was happening to our city."

At a busy bus stop, oncology nurse Olena Yehorova smiles at a gray-haired man playing folk music on his accordion.

"This truce has been such a relief," she says. "The people in our city have been able to breathe. Of course, we still walk around with caution, because you cannot trust the Russians."

She couldn't help looking up at the sky. A few hours later, the truce was over. She said she expects new attacks to resume at any time.

NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this report from Kyiv.

item.title: 6 books you won't want to miss in November
item.description: Welcome, one and all, to perhaps the only story you'll read today that's not awash in Election Day content. Now, that's not to say these books coming out in November dodge politics — everything is politics, to be clear — just that here, in this safe space, you may enjoy a rare reprieve from punditry, polling or horserace imagery.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome, one and all, to perhaps the only story you'll read today that's not awash in Election Day content.

Now, that's not to say these books coming out in November dodge politics — everything is politics, to be clear — just that here, in this safe space, you may enjoy a rare reprieve from punditry, polling or horserace imagery.

So take a deep breath, stretch your poor neck and shoulders, and relish imagining your carefree self a few days or weeks from now. Surely everything will have worked out by then (right?), and you'll be contentedly nosedeep in one of this month's notable books: immersed in stories of star-crossed romance or hard-won redemption, high-stakes struggle or sex-fueled farce.

Talking with All Things Considered in 2022, Kennedy described how it felt , after nearly three decades as a chef, to take up writing in earnest for the first time: "I just felt better somehow, which is kind of weird," observed Kennedy, describing the feeling as "strangely liberating." Now the Northern Irish author is returning with her sophomore effort. And like her debut, Trespasses , Kennedy's new book foregrounds the devastating fallout of an inauspicious young love, which struggles this time around not under the weight of religious difference but the long shadows of their family pasts.

In a review of Ask Again, Yes , which Keane published in 2019, Fresh Air book critic Maureen Corrigan compared the American writer to Ann Patchett : "Both have the magical ability to seem to be telling 'only' a closely-observed domestic tale that transforms into something else deep and, yes, universal." The ability showcased in that "modestly magnificent novel" is on display again in her latest novel, which, with the tale of an Irish father and his many sons, weaves a sweeping narrative that comes to encompass years, seas and continents.

O'Hara, a history professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz, leaves the territory typically trod by academics — research journals, conference keynotes — with this book that, though rooted in archival study, often reads like a swashbuckling adventure story. At the heart of it all is a poison – so notoriously lethal that it was known as "flying death" – called curare, which was deployed in blowdarts used by some Amazon tribes. As it turns out, the herbal mixture also was thought to have medicinal properties, the pursuit of which began in the 1930s, spanned continents, incited rivalries and opened new avenues in pharmacology — not to mention moneymaking — and indelibly impacted the tribes whose role has been all but forgotten.

Johnson's debut novel, Everything Under , earned her the mantle of youngest Booker Prize finalist ever, at 27 years old, when it appeared on the award's shortlist in 2018 . By now, the British writer has outgrown her wunderkind status, with another novel and a short story collection already under her belt. Long Wave fits well with the rest of Johnson's growing catalog — elusive images, spare prose, a foreboding atmosphere redolent of myth and mystery. And at the heart of it all, women whose family bonds they carry like broken glass, all aglitter with love and menace.

Make no mistake, Uprising sets a bleak scene: a river island in Bangladesh where women have been tricked, drugged, beaten and trapped in a life of prostitution they didn't choose. They're in thrall to a cruel madam, the men arriving nightly by boat and the inexorably rising waters of a region brutalized by climate change. But leaving the island is all but unthinkable, not only for them but their children fathered by customers. It's largely from the children's perspective that we hear this story, which, while bleak, isn't hopeless, as the arrival of a new girl has just set something in motion.

Unquestionably the strangest entry on this month's list, Amazons also happens to be the oldest. This ribald romp of ice hockey and sexy times first hit bookshelves more than four decades before Heated Rivalry ushered in the Era of Hockey Romance that we live in now. Which is notable, sure, but the strangeness is supplied by the name on the spine, Birdwell — she doesn't exist. The writer behind the pseudonym is the revered American novelist, Don DeLillo, who didn't publicly acknowledge having written it until 2020. The book itself developed a certain cult status even as copies became harder and harder to find at all. It wasn't until earlier this year that DeLillo OK'd its republication … with apparent reluctance, still. The sprightly comedy's only preface from him is a business card with his name below a brief statement: "I don't want to talk about it."

item.title: Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
item.description: MOGADISHU, Somalia — Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat and its crew of 20 hijacked off Somalia after an operation lasting more than 48 hours, India's Defense Ministry said Tuesday. The rescue of the Azini was completed Monday in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said.
item.content:encoded:
MOGADISHU, Somalia — Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat and its crew of 20 hijacked off Somalia after an operation lasting more than 48 hours, India's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.

The rescue of the Azini was completed Monday in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said.

An official with the Puntland Maritime Police Force told The Associated Press that Indian forces disarmed 12 suspected Somali pirates, confiscated their mobile phones and released them. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.

The suspects and two Somali security guards later came ashore at Bandar Bayla in northeastern Somalia, the official said. Three of those who came ashore had minor injuries, but he did not specify whether they were suspects or guards, or how they were hurt.

India's ministry said the operation ended without casualties or injuries. It did not specify whether that account covered everyone aboard or only the rescued crew. It was unclear whether the crew remained on the vessel or were moved elsewhere.

The operation involved a warship, a maritime surveillance aircraft and marine commandos. An Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft airdropped additional commandos, the ministry said.

The Azini was hijacked Oct. 29 between Bandar Bayla and Hafun. A Puntland maritime police officer said on Sunday that it carried 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. The difference between that crew count and India's rescue figure could not immediately be explained.

Indian forces tracked the vessel by sea and air before securing it, the ministry said. It said there had been concern that pirates could use the boat as a floating base for attacks on commercial ships.

The Puntland official said regional authorities learned of the rescue only after it had taken place.

The hijacking followed a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. By August, pirates had hijacked six commercial vessels since April, some far from Somalia's coast. They included the oil products tanker Sibu 1, seized about 252 kilometers (136 nautical miles) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen.

In September, Puntland authorities said pirates killed five crew members of the tanker MT Honour 25 before security forces recovered it. The tanker had been held since April. Authorities said they detained 16 suspected pirates.

The renewed piracy adds to shipping risks in a region already disrupted by the Iran war. Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and threats by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb have complicated oil transport routes.

Those disruptions have lengthened voyages and driven up tanker costs. Some oil shipments diverted around Africa face journeys up to a month longer.

International naval patrols and improved maritime security have sharply reduced Somali piracy over the past decade, but recent hijackings have renewed concerns about the threat.
